issues.item: Triggers: Power Imbalance: Being in a situation where someone has power over me
issues.explanation: The trigger 'being in a situation where someone has power over me' is hard to reconcile with the stated trauma type of natural disaster and with the rest of the profile, which otherwise emphasizes alarm/reactivity and fragmented recall rather than interpersonal domination or coercion. For this trauma type, this item introduces an implausible trigger theme not supported elsewhere in threat, memory, or appraisals.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
issues.explanation: Avoiding hospitals/ambulances/physical examinations is not well supported by the rest of the profile for a natural-disaster trauma. There are no memory or threat items involving injury treatment, medical rescue, or bodily harm, so this strategy appears to target a symptom theme not represented elsewhere. In contrast, the profile is centered on generalized alarm, shouting, unpredictability, and fragmented memory.

issues.item: Self-Harm: hurt myself physically to release overwhelming feelings
issues.explanation: Self-harm is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile and trauma context: the other selected items describe a classic hyperarousal/re-experiencing natural-disaster PTSD presentation with avoidance and overeating, but no accompanying items suggest the kind of shame, self-punitive appraisal, dissociative affect regulation, or broader emotion-dysregulation pattern that would make physical self-harm clinically coherent here. It stands out as addressing a symptom process not otherwise represented in the five components.

Alcohol smell is not impossible, but in this profile it is weakly anchored to the reported trauma type and the rest of the item set. The other triggers (unpredictability, shouting) fit a danger/hyperarousal formulation, whereas alcohol smell implies a very specific sensory trauma cue that is not supported by the memory or threat items. Given a natural-disaster index trauma, this trigger is difficult to explain clinically without additional corroborating content.

vignette: Marcus Thorne was fifty-five when the coast broke. He had been securing the shutters on his duplex, confident in his routine, when the storm surge hit faster than the emergency broadcasts had promised. The wind did not build; it arrived as a physical weight, slamming the siding in. Through the gaps in the plywood, he heard neighbors’ voices rise into shrill shouts, then cut off as a support wall collapsed. The roar was absolute, drowning out the sirens that should have directed them. He remembered the sudden shift in pressure, the way debris began to fall without warning, and the complete collapse of any structure that had promised safety. In that moment, the disaster was not just weather; it was the total violation of predictability, a chaos that left no time for preparation. When the waters receded, Marcus tried to file the event away. But the memory would not stay contained. He found himself pushing it out of his head the moment it began to surface, aware that he was only holding fragments—the screech of tearing metal, the sudden drop in his stomach, the shouting he could never quite hear clearly because the rest was simply missing. Whenever the pieces did break through, a hot, coiled rage flooded his chest, making his hands shake. His body had begun to react long before his mind could catch up. A backfiring car on the interstate would make him slam the brakes and grip the wheel, his heart hammering as if the roof were already tearing off. He lived with the constant certainty that the ground might give way again, reacting to every sudden sound as if the storm were returning. On two separate occasions, he had dropped a cup of coffee and braced himself against the kitchen counter, convinced he was back in the collapsing hallway, his muscles locking as the past replayed over his nervous system. Alongside the trembling in his hands, Marcus began eating through the evenings. He found himself standing over the stove or the pantry long after dinner, chewing through the tightness in his jaw and the pressure behind his ribs. He stopped accepting overtime at the bomb disposal unit, avoiding anything that required him to step into unstructured field conditions. When his wife, Elena, tried to discuss upcoming neighborhood maintenance or plan a family gathering, Marcus changed the subject or left the room, certain that any unresolved task would cascade into another sudden collapse. He kept his mind perpetually occupied, listening to engineering podcasts at high volume, solving crosswords, and scrolling through technical manuals, terrified that a quiet moment would let the storm back in. The habits solidified over months. His foreman noticed him declining calls to inspect compromised zones, citing a need to stay at the depot where he could control the environment. At home, the weight of his constant preoccupation and his sudden, unexplained departures left Elena wondering where he had gone, even when he was sitting right beside her. The breaking point came not with a storm, but with a dropped wrench in the training bay. The clang had sent him to the floor, knees buckling, before he could stop himself. That night, standing in the dim kitchen while Elena watched with quiet concern, Marcus knew his coping strategies were no longer shielding him. The overeating, the avoidance, and the mental noise existed side by side, each heavy in its own right. He had come to believe that if he did not find a way to anchor himself, he would lose his composure permanently, caught between the workshop floor and a past that refused to stay buried. He was seeking help not to erase the storm, but to stop his body from answering for it, hoping to reclaim the ability to stand still when the world suddenly grew loud. His intake assessment that week returned a score of sixty-four, a number that mirrored what he already felt: the weight of a threat that never fully lifted.
